summary: Captures the problem statement for the Softwires Working Group, which developed standards for connecting IPv4 networks across IPv6-only networks and the reverse. It describes discovery, control, and encapsulation needs. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Old and new Internet address systems cannot talk directly. This note describes the problem of making tunnels so one kind can cross the other.

questions: how to connect ipv4 networks over ipv6
subtitle: Standardizing tunnels to connect old and new Internet address systems

tldr.problem: IPv4 and IPv6 networks cannot interoperate directly, but the world needs both coexisting. Some networks run only IPv4, others only IPv6, and they need to exchange traffic across incompatible backbones.
tldr.mechanism: The Softwires Working Group developed standards for automatic tunnel discovery, control, and encapsulation to let IPv4 networks cross IPv6 backbones and IPv6 networks cross IPv4 backbones, solving two topologies: hub-and-spoke (simple, scalable) and mesh (general, complex).
tldr.outcome: This problem statement guided the development of softwire standards that became foundational for IPv6 transition, enabling networks to add IPv6 support gradually without replacing IPv4 infrastructure.

today: RFC 4925 is an informational RFC that defined the scope of the Softwires Working Group and remains the reference for softwire architecture. Its two scenarios—hub-and-spoke and mesh—became the basis for standards like Dual-Stack Lite (DS-Lite) for hub-and-spoke and Softwire Mesh for carrier-class deployments. As of 2026, both models continue to be used in production IPv6 transition strategies.

sections.title: The IPv4/IPv6 Coexistence Problem
sections.content:
The Internet is transitioning from IPv4 to IPv6, but the transition is neither instantaneous nor uniform. Networks upgrade at different times and rates. Some operators choose to run only IPv4 for cost reasons, others run only IPv6 as their new standard, and some have only certain devices that support one protocol or the other. Meanwhile, hosts and applications increasingly need to reach both IPv4 and IPv6 destinations.

A softwire is an automatically established tunnel that carries one address family through a network that natively supports only the other. Instead of manually configuring each tunnel, the softwire standards define discovery, control, and encapsulation mechanisms so that softwires can be set up dynamically when needed. This document identifies the two main network topologies that demand softwire solutions and specifies the requirements each imposes on a softwire system.
sections.plainLanguage: Both old and new address systems will exist for years. Networks that use only one need to send traffic to networks using the other. A softwire automatically wraps traffic in a tunnel so it crosses incompatible networks without manual configuration.

sections.title: Key Concepts and Terminology
sections.content:
A softwire is a tunnel with both control and data planes managed by a protocol. The Softwire Transport Header Address Family (STH AF) is the outermost address family—the network the tunnel crosses. The Softwire Payload Header Address Family (SPH AF) is the inner address family—what is being carried. For example, IPv6 packets tunneled through IPv4 have STH AF = IPv4 and SPH AF = IPv6.

The Softwire Initiator (SI) starts the tunnel, usually on the customer side. The Softwire Concentrator (SC) terminates it, usually on the carrier side. The concentrator aggregates many initiators, similar to an airline hub aggregating spoke routes. Softwires can also be arranged as a mesh, where each edge node tunnels directly to relevant peers.
sections.plainLanguage: A softwire has two ends: one where traffic enters (the initiator, usually the customer), and one where it exits (the concentrator, usually the carrier). The tunnel carries one address type through a network that uses another.

sections.title: Hubs and Spokes: Simple Scalable Connectivity
sections.content:
In the hub-and-spoke model, many customer networks (spokes) connect to a few central softwire concentrators (hubs). Each customer network initiates softwires to reach a concentrator. This model suits Internet service providers and enterprises where most traffic flows through central points. For example, a residential ISP might have millions of homes (spokes) each running IPv4, all needing IPv6 connectivity through a small number of carrier softwire concentrators.

The RFC identifies four variants based on which device initiates the softwire: the host CPE directly, the router CPE, a host behind an IPv4-only CPE, or a dedicated IPv6 device behind an IPv4-only CPE. It also addresses practical concerns: many CPE devices cannot be upgraded to dual-stack, so softwires must be initiated from a host inside the network. Softwires must traverse NAT (Network Address Translation), which adds complexity. The initiative must work seamlessly across dynamic IP address assignments and support features like DHCPv6 prefix delegation to give customers stable IPv6 address blocks.
sections.plainLanguage: Hub-and-spoke works when one big company (the hub) collects traffic from many small ones (the spokes). Each spoke office starts a tunnel to the hub. The hub does not need to change its customers' equipment; softwires can start from a computer inside the office.

sections.title: Mesh: General Routed Networks
sections.content:
In the mesh model, a backbone network that supports only one address family (say IPv6) must carry traffic for the other address family (IPv4) between customer networks. The backbone's core routers run only IPv6; the border routers run dual-stack and compute softwires between each other using BGP routing information. This model handles arbitrary topologies and scales to carrier-class networks where the backbone is shared among many customers with many interconnection points.

The mesh model does not require changes to core routers—only the border routers must understand both address families and perform encapsulation. It supports multiple encapsulations (L2TPv3, IP-in-IP, MPLS, GRE, IPsec) chosen by policy, multicast across the backbone by replication if needed, and diverse path computation for protection and load balancing.
sections.plainLanguage: Mesh is for larger networks where traffic does not funnel through a few hubs. Routers at the edges of the backbone tunnel traffic through it. The backbone itself does not need to change, only the routers at the borders.

sections.title: Common Requirements Across Both Models
sections.content:
Both models require automatic softwire setup without extensive provisioning, scalability to millions of initiators (hubs and spokes) or many routing prefixes (mesh), and support for multicast and dynamic address management. They both need keepalive mechanisms to detect tunnel failures across NAT and other intermediate devices, and operations and management (OAM) features including logging, accounting, and performance monitoring.

Security is critical. In hubs and spokes, the protocol must authenticate customers and authorize their access. In mesh, peers on different networks must mutually authenticate. Both require privacy and integrity protection, with IPsec as a mandatory option. The RFC emphasizes that softwire setup time must be very small—a fraction of total startup time—so they are practical for dynamic connections.
sections.plainLanguage: Both hub-and-spoke and mesh need softwires that start quickly, detect when they break, let operators see what is happening, and protect traffic from eavesdropping.

sections.title: Encapsulation and Transition Strategy
sections.content:
The RFC identifies IPv6/IPv4, IPv6/UDP/IPv4, and IPv4/IPv6 as critical encapsulation types. The choice of which encapsulation to use depends on policy, packet characteristics, and softwire endpoint capabilities. The flexibility to support multiple encapsulations is essential because different scenarios have different constraints: some require IPsec for security, others use GRE for simplicity, and mesh networks may use MPLS for traffic engineering.

The softwire standards aim to reuse existing technology (tunneling mechanisms, DHCP, routing protocols) rather than invent new protocols. This keeps time-to-market short—critical because operators needed IPv6 deployment solutions years ago. The working group explicitly decided to divide the overall problem into hubs-and-spokes and mesh rather than create one monolithic solution, allowing simpler protocols for hub-and-spoke while retaining full flexibility for mesh.
sections.plainLanguage: Softwires can wrap packets in different ways depending on what the network needs. Some need IPsec encryption, others do not. Some networks use MPLS, others use simpler IP tunnels. The standards support all of these.

left.title: Hub-and-Spoke
left.desc: Many customer networks initiate tunnels to a few carrier hubs. Simple, scalable, but traffic must flow through hubs.

right.title: Mesh
right.desc: Border routers tunnel directly between each other. Supports arbitrary topologies but more complex routing.
